RSFX 5311 · Fixed Prosthodontics I

Review of Principles and Practical Protocols for Testing Monolithic Zirconia

The full coverage indirect restoration on #3, item by item: why each standard exists, what the patient pays when it is missed, and how we test it on the practical.

Rafael Rocha Pacheco, DDS, MSc, PhDAssociate Dean for Digital Technologies and Associate Professor
Section Director of Dental Materials, Department of Restorative Sciences
Dental College of Georgia at Augusta University

Behavioral objectives RubricFinal remarks

By the end of this review you should be able to

Must know, 10Good to know, 5Nice to know, 3
1MustExplain why a full coverage indirect restoration is made: it can be made outside the mouth, not because the tooth is weak or the lesion is large.2MustRelate every rubric item to one of four jobs: seat, stay, survive, stay healthy.3MustState the occlusal clearance standard of 1.5 mm and predict the result of too little or too much.4MustDescribe the functional cusp bevel on #3 and what happens to the restoration without it.5MustDistinguish taper (one wall) from total occlusal convergence (two opposing walls) and state the 12 to 16° target.6MustExplain why every opposing pair, MB-DL and ML-DB included, must converge, and what makes a pair an undercut.7MustExplain how axial wall height and the resistance groove stop the restoration from tipping off.8MustDescribe the 0.8 mm chamfer and the 140° cavosurface angle, and what a feather edge or bevel does to zirconia.9MustExplain why line angles are rounded and axial walls finished smooth for a milled restoration.10MustApply the six-step measurement protocol to grade a preparation before raising your hand.11GoodExplain why monolithic zirconia tolerates thin sections yet still depends on preparation geometry for retention.12GoodIdentify the long axis of the planned restoration as the reference for the path of insertion, not a tipped tooth or its neighbors.13GoodRecognize a barrel-shaped axial wall and explain why a scanner cannot see under it.14GoodExplain the periodontal and digital reasons for a supragingival margin and untouched neighbors.15GoodDescribe how deviations become deductions and a letter grade on the practical.16NiceRecall that students cut about 13° of convergence on typodonts and 23° on patients.17NiceDescribe why a chairside mill may need up to 0.5 mm more occlusal reduction than the guideline.18NiceList the treatment management items and the two that cost 10 points.
The premise RubricFinal remarks

Your hands are rarely the problem. Not seeing why is.

Once you can explain why 15°, why the bevel, why the groove stops 1 mm short of the margin, your hands follow. This review trains the eye first.

The first question RubricFinal remarksBO 1

Why are you even making a crown?

Two common answers, and the real one
1"The tooth cannot hold a restoration that large." Not the reason: large multi-surface posterior resin composite restorations are a documented long-term option; risk rises with each surface.34
2"It makes the tooth stronger." Not the reason: the preparation removes far more sound tooth than partial coverage.27 Coverage protects what remains (endodontically treated teeth without it were lost at about 6 times the rate), but tooth structure is not made stronger.35,2
3"Because I can make it outside the mouth." The real reason: anatomy, contacts and occlusion designed and checked, and materials processed in ways the mouth cannot offer.33,9
Where it is made
In the mouthOutside the mouth
AnatomyCarved against the clock in a wet fieldDesigned and checked on a model or in software
MaterialLight-cured in placeSintered in a furnace; dense industrial blocks
OcclusionAdjusted after placementDesigned against the opposing arch
MarginsShaped in placeFitted to a die or a scan

Sources. [2] Shillingburg, Ch. 10. [9] Turkyilmaz et al. J Dent Sci 2021. [27] Edelhoff, Sorensen. Int J Periodontics Restorative Dent 2002. [33] Pacheco RR, Rocha MG. Phillips' 14th ed., Ch. 15. [34] Opdam et al. J Dent Res 2014. [35] Aquilino, Caplan. J Prosthet Dent 2002.

A better name RubricFinal remarks

Not a crown. A full coverage indirect restoration.

"Crown" invites the wrong reasons. The full name says what you are making and why it is made this way.

Full coverage
Every axial surface is encircled, so retention comes from opposing external walls.1
Indirect
Made outside the mouth in its final form, so it must go back on along one path of insertion.1
Restoration
It replaces lost form and function; it does not cure the disease that caused the loss.2
The one idea to keep
The restoration exists because it can be made outside the mouth. Every preparation rule exists so that it can go back in, seat, stay, survive and keep the tissues healthy.
Reading the rubric RubricFinal remarksBO 2

Every rubric item does one of four jobs

Shillingburg's principles of tooth preparation, written as what the restoration has to do once it leaves the laboratory.1 Click a card.

Two more jobs for a milled restoration. The scanner must see the whole finish line,22 and the milling bur, about 1.0 to 1.3 mm wide, must be able to reach every internal corner.9

The material RubricFinal remarksBO 11 BO 17

Strong enough to be thin, too inert to bond casually

What it means for the preparation
1Monolithic zirconia molar restorations at 0.5 mm exceeded physiologic molar loads in vitro.4,5
2Translucent 4Y and 5Y grades keep only about 75% and 50% tetragonal phase: less transformation toughening, strength near lithium disilicate, single units only.6,41
3Polished monolithic zirconia does not wear enamel excessively; glazed zirconia does once the glaze wears through. Polish after every adjustment.41
43Y-TZP: flexural strength 900 to 1500 MPa, fracture toughness above 5 MPa·m½, modulus 210 GPa; a crack tip triggers the tetragonal-to-monoclinic change that squeezes it shut.38
5Grinding or sandblasting triggers the same change at the surface: compressive now, possibly tensile later. Adjust gently, polish, follow the manufacturer.38
6Zirconia has no glass phase to etch; bonding needs particle abrasion and phosphate monomer primers.7
7Cemented conventionally, it is held by taper, height and grooves.1
Three numbers
0.5mmThickness that still survivedWe ask for 1.5 mm as a safety margin.4,5
0.5mmExtra reduction a chairside mill may needOvermilling eats the planned thickness.8
12°Convergence with the best coping fitBetter than 4° or 8°.10

Sources. [1] Shillingburg, Ch. 9. [4] Nakamura et al. Acta Odontol Scand 2015. [5] Sorrentino et al. J Mech Behav Biomed Mater 2016. [6] Zhang, Lawn. J Dent Res 2018. [7] Blatz et al. J Dent Res 2018. [8] Skordou et al. J Osseointegr 2021. [10] Beuer et al. Quintessence Int 2009. [38] Craig's, Ch. 11: transformation toughening, properties of 3Y-TZP, metastability after grinding. [41] Phillips 13th, Ch. 10: 4Y and 5Y phase content, wear of opposing enamel, occlusal adjustment.

Rubric item 1 · Occlusal reduction RubricGauge labMore about zirconiaFinal remarksBO 3

Clearance is the restoration's thickness

Standard1.5 mm at B cusp, CG, marginal ridges, L cuspStandardFCB and wall junction inside the projected contourCriticalunder 1 mm

GPT-10 Occlusal reduction: the quantity of tooth structure removed to make space for the restorative material. Interocclusal clearance: the space that reduction achieved for an adequate thickness of material.39

Why it exists
1Inadequate occlusal reduction is a common cause of ceramic fracture; most ceramic crowns want 2.0 mm, monolithic zirconia tolerates less, and the manufacturer's guideline rules.41,1
2Fracture load of monolithic zirconia falls as occlusal thickness falls.4
31.5 mm absorbs overmilling, occlusal adjustment and weaker translucent grades.8,6
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Under 1 mm: perforation on adjustment, or a bulked, high restoration.1
2Over 2 mm: shorter axial walls, less retention and resistance.1,3
3Over 2 mm: more tooth lost and a closer pulp; loss of vitality is a documented late complication.27,28
How we test
1Condenser gauge in MI: the 1.5 mm end first, then the 2 mm end, held parallel to the cusp inclines, never flat across the occlusal. 1.5 does not pass: under-reduced. 2 passes with room: over 2 mm.32
2Perio probe tip (0.8 mm) tight: under 1 mm, critical.32
3Bite registration silicone (Blu-Mousse) set between the arches, then a caliper on it gives the number.32
We measure clearance, not reduction
The gauge reads the space the restoration will occupy, between preparation and opposing tooth in MI. It does not read how much tooth you cut. Measure the space, not the effort.39
Figures

Sources. [39] GPT-10: occlusal reduction, interocclusal clearance. [41] Phillips 13th, Ch. 10: inadequate occlusal reduction is a common cause of ceramic fracture. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [3] Goodacre et al. J Prosthet Dent 2001. [4] Nakamura 2015. [6] Zhang, Lawn 2018. [8] Skordou 2021. [27] Edelhoff, Sorensen 2002. [28] Cheung et al. Int Endod J 2005. [30] Kateeb et al. Eur J Dent Educ 2017. [37] Craig's, Ch. 4: with a weaker material, reduce stress by increasing its bulk. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric v10.15.23.

Rubric items 2 and 3 · Bevel and contours RubricFinal remarksBO 4

Follow the tooth's planes, bevel the cusp that works

StandardFCB 45 to 60° on the palatal cuspStandardCusps and CG aligned with opposing anatomyStandardOriginal cusp angles keptCriticalno FCB
Why it exists
1On #3 the palatal cusp is functional; its bevel gives bulk where contact is heaviest.1,2
2The bevel angle follows the inclination of the opposing cusps.2
3Inclined planes give clearance without shortening; splitting one corner into two faces also spreads the load.1,11,37
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1No bevel: a thin or perforated restoration at the occluso-axial junction.1
2No bevel, bulked out: overcontour and a deflective contact.1
3Flat table or steep bevel: a short preparation or an over-inclined wall.1
How we test
1Mesial view in MI: bevel parallel to the opposing buccal cusp incline.2
2The same 2 mm wax shows clearance over the palatal cusp.2
3Cusp angles compared with the unprepared #2 and #14.32
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [11] Habib et al. J Adv Prosthodont 2014. [37] Craig's, Ch. 4. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric v10.15.23.

Rubric items 4 and 19 · Angles and finish RubricMore about zirconiaFinal remarksBO 9

Round it for the bur, finish it for the fit

StandardLine and point angles roundedStandardDiamond-textured, not rough or polishedStandardAxial walls flat planesCriticalsharp line or point angles

GPT-10 Line angle: the point of convergence of two planes in a tooth preparation.39

Why it exists
1Stress is force over area, and the peak stress at a corner rises with the square root of its length over its tip radius: the sharper the corner, the higher the peak, and a ceramic fails from that point.37,40
2Give every internal line angle as large a radius as possible; a milling bur about 1.0 to 1.3 mm wide cannot cut tighter than its own radius anyway.40,9
3Finishing burs gave the smallest marginal gaps; polishing the preparation is not needed.13,14
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Sharp corners: a stress riser where bending puts the ceramic in tension; the software also overmills so the restoration rocks.41,9,8
2Rough or faceted walls: high spots hold the restoration up.13
3Polished walls: less mechanical interlock for the cement.14
How we test
1Explorer dragged across every junction should glide.32
2Loupes at 2.5x to 3.5x with light at an angle.25
3Scan sections show corners and facets as kinks.30
Same force, smaller area, higher stress
A shoe on your foot hurts; a high heel hurts more, same weight. A sharp knife cuts, a dull one does not. Stress is force over area,37,40 so a sharp line angle in ceramic is that heel, that edge. Round it; a bevel does the same by making one corner into two faces.2
Figures

Sources. [39] GPT-10. [2] Shillingburg Ch. 10. [40] Phillips 13th, Ch. 4: stress at a flaw rises with √(length/tip radius); round internal line angles. [41] Phillips, Ch. 10: sharp line angles are stress risers in the restoration. [37] Craig's, Ch. 4: stress = force/area; avoid sharp line angles and notches to limit stress concentration. [8] Skordou 2021. [9] Turkyilmaz et al. J Dent Sci 2021. [13] Ayad. J Prosthodont 2009. [14] Krishna et al. Cureus 2024. [25] Badar et al. Indian J Dent Res 2019. [30] Kateeb 2017. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 5 and 11 · Axial reduction RubricFinal remarks

Room for the wall, all the way around

Standard0.8 mm on B, L, M and DStandardEven depth around the toothCritical0.0 mm on L, M or D
Why it exists
1Axial reduction creates space for an adequate thickness of restoration wall.1
2Uneven depth around the tooth worsens zirconia marginal fit.12
3Full coverage already removes a large share of coronal tooth; extra depth costs more.27
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Under: thin walls, or an overcontour that inflames the gingiva.1
2Over: a weaker cervical tooth and a closer pulp.27,28
3Stopped at the contact: a ledge under the contact area.1
How we test
1Perio probe tip (0.8 mm) laid against the axial wall, perpendicular to the long axis; look from the occlusal with one eye closed.32
2Margin ends exactly at the edge of the tip: 0.8 mm. Margin shows past the tip: about 1.0 mm. Only half the tip over margin: about 0.4 mm, under-reduced.32
3Scan section against the unprepared contour; expect the usual pattern, buccal over and lingual under.30,32
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [12] Azar et al. Int J Prosthodont 2011. [27] Edelhoff, Sorensen 2002. [28] Cheung 2005. [30] Kateeb 2017. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 6 and 13 · Plane of reduction RubricGauge labFinal remarksBO 13

Flat walls, no barrel

StandardB/L walls flat O-G, even M-DStandardM/D walls flat, not undercutCriticalundercut
Why it exists
1Retention needs two opposing walls in one path.1
2A flat wall keeps its whole height useful for retention.1
3The needle diamond follows the contact bulge and leaves a cervical barrel.2
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Barrel: overtapered occlusally, undercut cervically.1
2Cervical undercut: the restoration will not seat.1
3Scan shadow: a blocked-out zone and a thick cement line.22
How we test
1Survey each wall with one eye closed.1
2Mesial and buccal views of each profile.32
3Scan cross section through the wall.30
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [22] Casucci et al. Materials 2023. [30] Kateeb 2017. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 7, 8 and 12 · Convergence RubricGauge labFinal remarksBO 5

Why 15°, and why MB must converge with DL

StandardTOC 12 to 16°, 6 to 8° taper per wallStandardB-L, M-D and every line angleStandardPath along the restoration's long axisCriticalovertaper over 25°; undercut

GPT-10 Taper: the angle between one external wall and the path of placement. Total occlusal convergence: the total angle formed by opposing axial walls, as viewed in a given plane.39

Why it exists
1Taper is one wall against the path of insertion; total occlusal convergence is the angle between two opposing walls, the sum of both tapers.1,3
2Every opposing pair, B-L, M-D, MB-DL and ML-DB, must converge; about 12° TOC guarantees no undercut.1,16
316° TOC keeps adequate retention, and zirconia copings fit better at 12° than at 4° or 8°.1,10
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Over 25°: many paths of withdrawal; the restoration debonds.1
2Diverging diagonal: corners are cut in separate passes, so undercuts hide there.32,1
3Path tilted M or D: locked out by the adjacent contacts.1
How we test
1One eye closed at about 30 cm; both eyes open can hide 8°.1
2Survey both axes and both diagonals.1
3Angle measured on scan sections.30
Figures

Sources. [1] Shillingburg Ch. 9. [3] Goodacre 2001. [10] Beuer et al. Quintessence Int 2009. [16] Mack. J Oral Rehabil 1980. [30] Kateeb 2017. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 9, 10 and 14 · Height and groove RubricGauge labFinal remarksBO 7

Height and a groove stop the tipping arc

Standard4.0 mm B, 3.5 mm L, 3.0 mm M and DStandardGroove mid-lingual, parallel, 1 mm above marginCriticalgroove undercut or missing

GPT-10 Retention form resists dislodgment along the path of placement; resistance form resists dislodgment along any other axis.39

Why it exists
1Walls must block the arc of a restoration pivoting on the opposite margin.1
2Minimum 4 mm on molars and 3 mm on other teeth, at 10 to 20°.3
3A groove in the bulkiest wall prevents rotation; grooves gave complete resistance on short 15° dies.2,18
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Short walls: it tips and debonds; only 46% of molar preparations had resistance form.1,17
2V-shaped groove: about half the resistance.19
3Groove into the margin: a notched finish line.32
How we test
1Probe margin to occlusal at mid B, L, M and D.32
2Probe from the groove end to the margin: 1 mm.32
3Survey the groove with one eye; it parallels the walls.1
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [3] Goodacre 2001. [17] Parker et al. J Prosthet Dent 1991. [18] Woolsey, Matich. JADA 1978. [19] Kishimoto et al. J Prosthet Dent 1983. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 16 and 18 · Margin geometry RubricGauge labMore about zirconiaFinal remarksBO 8

A chamfer gives an edge with bulk behind it

Standard0.8 mm chamferStandardCavosurface angle 140°Criticalacute (under 90°); slice or feather; beveled

GPT-10 Chamfer: a finish line where the gingival aspect meets the external axial surface at an obtuse angle. Cavosurface angle: the angle at the junction of prepared and unprepared tooth.39

Why it exists
1The chamfer combines an acute edge with nearby bulk and low stress.1
2Zirconia copings on a chamfer resisted fracture better than on a shoulder.20
3140° leaves about a 40° zirconia edge; margins near the path of insertion seat worse.32,21
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Narrow or feather: a chippy edge and an overcontoured cervical third.1
2Lip, the J margin: an acute sliver of tooth left at the cavosurface. Acute angles concentrate stress, and in enamel the rods run from the DEJ out to the surface, so anything under 90° leaves rods with nothing under them. It snaps at cementation or in function and leaves an open margin.1,37,42
3Wide: cervical tooth lost. Bevel: an unsupported ceramic edge.1
How we test
1Probe the width at M, B, D and L.32
2Edge-on view for a lip, bevel or feather.1
3Scan cross section at each site.30
Figures

Sources. [1] Shillingburg Ch. 9. [4] Nakamura 2015. [20] Jalalian et al. J Dent (Tehran) 2011. [21] Ostlund. Oper Dent 1985. [30] Kateeb 2017. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 15, 17 and 20 · Margin location RubricFinal remarksBO 14

Above the gingiva, clear of the neighbors

StandardMargin 0.3 to 0.5 mm supragingival, smoothStandardNo damage to gingiva or neighborsCriticalgross damage to a neighbor
Why it exists
1Supragingival margins can be finished, cleaned and recorded.1
2Intraoral scanners lose accuracy at subgingival margins.22
3Margins within 2 mm of the alveolar crest invade the attachment.24
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Subgingival: inflammation; defects up to 120 µm missed.1,23
2Nicked neighbor: found on 78% of mesial neighbors; plaque and caries risk.25,26
3Lacerated gingiva: blood in the sulcus spoils the scan.22
How we test
1Probe from the gingival crest at each site.32
2Loupes on the neighbors and the tissue.25
3Prevent it: needle diamond first, enamel sliver last.2
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [22] Casucci 2023. [23] Christensen. J Prosthet Dent 1966. [24] Gargiulo et al. J Periodontol 1961. [25] Badar 2019. [26] Moopnar, Faulkner. Aust Dent J 1991. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric.

Rubric items 21 to 25 · Treatment management RubricFinal remarksBO 18

The parts of the grade that are about you

StandardTight MIStandardDentoform clean, completeStandard#3 onlyStandardCorrect positionStandardOn timeCriticalwrong tooth; desk not cleared (−10 each)
Why it exists
1Clearance and bevel checks are only valid against the true opposing arch.2
2Surveying needs a stable view; poor posture drives musculoskeletal disorders.1,29
3Verification and a clean field are professional habits.32
If it goes wrongClinical outcome
1Loose MI: false clearance readings.2
2Wrong tooth: −10 and a healthy tooth prepared.32
3Desk not cleared before removing the dentoform: −10.32
How we test
1Close in MI before and after preparing.32
2Read the tooth number before the first cut.32
3Components tight, bar removed, desk clear.32
Figures

Sources. [1,2] Shillingburg Ch. 9, 10. [29] Hayes et al. Int J Dent Hyg 2009. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric v10.15.23.

Practical protocol RubricFinal remarksBO 10 BO 16

How a preparation is tested, in order

Grade your own preparation in this sequence before you raise your hand. It is the order the grader follows.

1
Verify
Correct tooth; dentoform seated and closed in tight MI.32
2
Clearance
Condenser gauge, 1.5 then 2 mm, along the cusp inclines in MI; probe tip for under 1 mm; silicone and caliper for a number.32
3
Survey
One eye closed at about 30 cm: every pair, the path, the groove.1
4
Measure
Probe: margin width, wall height, groove position, distance to the crest.32
5
Inspect
Loupes and explorer: margin, angles, neighbors, gingiva.25
6
Scan
Superimpose on the unprepared tooth; Planmeca Compare is being piloted here.30
Why the self-check matters
Students cut about 13° of convergence on typodonts and about 23° on patients. What you learn to see here is what transfers.1,31

Sources. [1] Shillingburg Ch. 9. [2] Shillingburg Ch. 10. [25] Badar 2019. [30] Kateeb 2017. [31] Weed et al. J Dent Res 1984. [32] RSFX 5311 rubric v10.15.23.

The rubric RubricBO 15

How deviations become a grade

Deduction levelsPer section, one cap per range
1Standard. Meets every specification: 0.32
2Minor. −1 to −4, for example clearance over 1.5 mm or taper 17 to 20°.32
3Moderate. −4.5 to −6, for example clearance under 1.5 mm or taper 21 to 24°.32
4Major. −6.5 to −8, for example taper over 25°.32
5Critical. −10, bold on the sheet, for example under 1 mm of clearance or the wrong tooth.32
The ladder: four sections, one cap each
60A bold item in every sectionOcclusal, buccal-lingual, proximal, margins: −10 each, the floor.32
68No bold, a major in every sectionStill failing, but 8 points up just by avoiding bold.32
76No majors, a moderate in every sectionA C. Avoid the moderates next.32
84No moderates, a minor in every sectionA B with four minors; the minors are the last thing to chase.32
Aim in this order
The sheet caps each section at one maximum per range, so the worst mark in a section is what you pay. Climb the ladder: no bold first, then no majors, then no moderates; do not lose sleep over every minor. And do not give points away: the functional cusp bevel, the retention groove and a clean desk are bold −10s, and in the clinic the first two are a restoration that fails.

Sources. [32] RSFX 5311 Practical #4 to #6, Zirconia Crown #3 rubric, version 10.15.23.
